questions.title: Why is a ternary weight alphabet described as 1.58 bits? Do real systems actually store 1.58 bits per weight?
questions.question_body: The paper says every weight takes values in {-1, 0, +1} and calls the model '1.58-bit' because log2(3) ≈ 1.585. In practice, memory is byte-addressable and kernels typically pack into whole numbers of bits. Are the weights actually stored in 2 bits per parameter during runtime, or is there a custom packing scheme that approaches 1.58 bits on average? If 2-bit storage is used, how should we interpret '1.58 bits' in the reported memory savings?

questions.title: Does BitNet b1.58 keep any parameters in full precision (e.g., embeddings, RMSNorm gains), or are truly all weights ternary?
questions.question_body: The abstract claims 'every single parameter (or weight) of the LLM is ternary {-1, 0, 1}', but in the Results section it says 'the embedding remains full precision.' Also, RMSNorm typically has learned scale parameters. Are token embeddings, positional embeddings/rotary parameters, RMSNorm scales, and SwiGLU gates all ternary in BitNet b1.58? If not, which components are exceptions, in what precision are they stored/used, and how much do they contribute to the overall memory footprint?

questions.title: How exactly is the absmean quantization with RoundClip applied and updated during training?
questions.question_body: The quantization is defined as \(\widetilde{W} = \mathrm{RoundClip}(W/(\gamma+\epsilon), -1, 1)\) with \(\gamma = \frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij}|W_{ij}|\). Do they compute \(\gamma\) once per forward pass per weight matrix, or is it updated less frequently (e.g., per step or per epoch)? Is \(\gamma\) computed per-tensor, per-row, or per-column? How sensitive is performance to the choice of per-tensor vs per-channel scaling?

questions.title: What gradient estimator is used to backpropagate through RoundClip and the ternary quantization?
questions.question_body: The paper quantizes weights via a non-differentiable RoundClip. During training from scratch with 1.58-bit weights, what estimator is used for gradients? Is it a straight-through estimator (STE), and if so, what exact form (e.g., identity through the rounding and clipping range and zero outside)? Do they keep a latent real-valued weight copy for updates, or are updates applied directly in the ternary space?

questions.title: How are activations quantized to 8-bit 'per token' and how is the scale handled across layers and KV cache?
questions.question_body: The paper states activations are 8-bit and 'scaled to [-Q_b, Q_b] per token' to avoid zero-point quantization. Does 'per token' mean a separate symmetric scale per sequence position (i.e., per row in the batch*time dimension), or per token per channel? How is the scale tracked and applied across consecutive layers, especially around non-linearities (SwiGLU) and attention softmax? What precision is used to store the KV cache, and is the same per-token scaling applied to cached keys/values across timesteps?

questions.title: Where do multiplications remain in BitNet b1.58, and what is the exact compute pathway for a ternary matmul?
questions.question_body: The paper says 'almost no multiplication operations' and that most compute becomes INT8 additions. For a linear layer \(y = \widetilde{W}x\) with \(\widetilde{W} \in \{-1,0,1\}^{m\times n}\), is the computation implemented as conditional adds/subtracts of \(x\), plus a final rescale by \(\gamma\)? If weights are encoded using a 2-bit kernel from Ladder, how is the multiply-by-\(-1\) implemented efficiently? Where precisely do any remaining multiplications occur (e.g., scaling by \(\gamma\), activation rescaling, layernorm, softmax), and in what precision?

questions.title: What accumulation precision is used for ternary matmuls? Is INT8 addition sufficient without overflow?
questions.question_body: A dot product involves summing up to \(n\) terms, which commonly requires INT32 accumulators to avoid overflow and preserve accuracy. The paper states the majority of BitNet b1.58 arithmetic is INT8 additions. Are partial sums kept in INT32 and then requantized, or are there techniques to keep accumulation in INT8 safely? Can the authors clarify the precise accumulator width for the main GEMM kernels?

questions.title: Why does adding the zero weight improve 'feature filtering' and modeling capacity relative to binary weights?
questions.question_body: The paper claims the inclusion of 0 in weights leads to explicit support for feature filtering and significantly improves performance over 1-bit (binary) models. Can you provide an intuitive explanation or formal argument for why allowing zero improves representational capacity or optimization? Do you have measurements of learned weight sparsity over training (e.g., ternary distribution over {-1, 0, 1}) and ablations that correlate sparsity with downstream performance?

questions.title: How is quantization applied around SwiGLU and RMSNorm, and are those parameters/activations also quantized?
questions.question_body: The architecture uses RMSNorm and SwiGLU. Are the RMSNorm weights (scales) and SwiGLU projection weights ternary as well? Are the activations feeding into and coming out of the SwiGLU nonlinearity quantized to 8-bit with symmetric per-token scales? How is numerical stability ensured for the RMS normalization and the GELU-like nonlinearity under 8-bit activation quantization?

questions.title: What is Q_b for 8-bit activations and does per-token symmetric scaling impact cross-token operations?
questions.question_body: When scaling activations to [-Q_b, Q_b], is Q_b set to 127 for signed int8? If each token uses its own symmetric scale, how does this interact with operations that mix tokens, like attention softmax across a sequence? Do you rescale to a common dynamic range before attention scores are computed, or are scores computed in higher precision after dequantization?

questions.title: How fair is the latency comparison given BitNet b1.58 uses a 2-bit optimized kernel while FP16 uses standard kernels?
questions.question_body: The results use FasterTransformer with the Ladder 2-bit kernel for BitNet b1.58. For FP16 baselines, what kernels and fused ops were enabled? Were both sides equally optimized (e.g., tensor cores, fused attention, flash-decoding)? Could kernel maturity explain part of the 2.4x–4.1x speedups, or do the authors have ablations controlling for kernel-level optimizations?

questions.title: How is 'matching full precision starting from 3B parameters' measured, and is the effect consistent across tasks?
questions.question_body: The paper states BitNet b1.58 matches FP16 LLaMA baselines in perplexity and downstream performance from 3B parameters, trained on 100B tokens. Which exact model configs (depth/width, vocab, tokenizer) were used for the matched comparisons? Are there tasks where the ternary model still lags notably even at 3B? Could you provide confidence intervals or multiple training runs to show robustness of 'matching' claims?

questions.title: Does the 'new scaling law' have a formal functional form, or is it an empirical equivalence table?
questions.question_body: The paper claims 'BitNet b1.58 is enabling a new scaling law' and lists equivalences like '13B b1.58 is more efficient than 3B FP16.' Is there a quantitative law relating model size, bit-precision, and inference cost/performance (e.g., \(\mathrm{cost} \propto N^\alpha / b^\beta\))? Or are the provided equivalences purely empirical on the tested hardware/software stack? If there is a law, what are the fitted exponents and assumptions?

questions.title: How were energy savings estimated (71.4x on 7nm), and what components are included or excluded?
questions.question_body: Figure estimates claim 71.4x arithmetic energy savings for matrix multiplication based on prior energy models. Does this include only MAC/ALU energy or also memory hierarchy (SRAM/DRAM) access energy? In end-to-end inference, how much of the total energy is actually spent on arithmetic vs memory for the tested sequence lengths? Do the measured end-to-end energy reductions align with the 71.4x arithmetic estimate, or are they smaller due to memory-bound behavior?

questions.title: Are KV caches quantized to 8-bit during decoding, and how does this affect long-context stability?
questions.question_body: The paper suggests 8-bit activations and mentions potential for further lossless compression for long contexts. In the reported latency/memory results, are the key/value caches stored in int8 during generation, or kept in FP16/BF16 for compatibility? If quantized, what is the scaling scheme for KV caches across timesteps (per-head, per-token, per-channel)? Any observed degradation in attention quality for long sequence lengths due to cache quantization?

questions.title: Why choose ternary {-1, 0, +1} rather than a 2-bit set like {-2, -1, +1, +2} or learned ternary thresholds?
questions.question_body: The paper uses RoundClip on W/(gamma+epsilon) to snap to {-1,0,+1}. Did you compare against other low-bit alphabets with 2 bits of dynamic range, or ternary with learned thresholds and scales per channel? What guided the choice of the absmean normalization and uniform ternary thresholds versus per-channel learned scales that might better match weight distributions?

questions.title: How is attention softmax computed under 8-bit activations: quantized or in higher precision?
questions.question_body: Attention involves computing \(QK^T / \sqrt{d}\), softmax, and then a weighted sum with \(V\). In BitNet b1.58, are Q, K, V projections ternary while Q, K, V activations are int8? Is the dot-product and softmax computed in FP16/FP32 after dequantizing activations, or performed partly in integer arithmetic? What precision and scaling is used to ensure numerical stability for softmax and to avoid underflow/overflow?

questions.title: What optimizer, learning rate schedule, and regularization are used to stabilize training from scratch with ternary weights?
questions.question_body: Training from scratch with 1.58-bit weights can be tricky. Could the authors share details on the optimizer (e.g., AdamW vs Lion), learning rate schedule, warmup, weight decay, gradient clipping, and any additional regularizers or tricks (e.g., stochastic rounding, noise, EMA)? Were there differences from FP16 LLaMA training recipes needed to prevent divergence or to reach parity?

questions.title: How does BitNet b1.58 integrate with common toolchains (HuggingFace, vLLM, llama.cpp) given custom kernels?
questions.question_body: The paper says BitNet b1.58 uses LLaMA-like components and can be integrated into popular stacks with minimal effort. Practically: do you provide a reference implementation of BitLinear modules with the 2-bit Ladder kernel, quantization-aware checkpoints, and export paths to GGUF or other formats? What are the main caveats when running on vLLM or llama.cpp (e.g., need for custom build flags, limited quantized attention kernels)?

questions.title: In MoE scenarios, which tensors dominate inter-chip traffic and how much does 8-bit activation quantization help?
questions.question_body: The Discussion suggests 1.58-bit LLMs reduce MoE communication overhead. For top-k routing, most all-to-all traffic is activations. If activations are already 8-bit, what is the measured bandwidth reduction compared to FP16 for realistic MoE setups (number of experts, capacity factor)? Are router logits and auxiliary losses computed in higher precision? Any empirical throughput/latency measurements showing the reduction in all-to-all time with BitNet b1.58?

questions.title: How were latency numbers measured: prefill vs decode, sequence lengths, batch sizes, and sampling overhead?
questions.question_body: The paper reports 'time per output token' using FasterTransformer. Was this measured in the decode phase with KV cache, or averaged across prefill+decode? What sequence length and batch size were used, and were tokens generated with greedy or with sampling (which can add overhead)? Are the reported speedups consistent across a range of batch sizes and context lengths, or do they vary significantly?

questions.title: Does adding zeros reduce energy further than binary weights, and why does the paper say energy is 'the same' as 1-bit?
questions.question_body: Intuitively, allowing 0 should skip some additions compared to binary {-1, +1}, potentially reducing energy further. However, the paper states 'it has the same energy consumption as the original 1-bit BitNet.' Are zeros actually skipped in kernels, and if so, why would the energy be the same? Is the statement meant in an asymptotic or worst-case sense rather than measured practice?

questions.title: For the 2T-token training comparison against StableLM-3B, how were data recipe and evaluation matched?
questions.question_body: You compare a BitNet b1.58 model trained for 2T tokens to StableLM-3B's reported numbers on a benchmark (Winogrande, PIQA, SciQ, LAMBADA, ARC-easy). Were tokenizer, data filtering, and sampling policies identical? Since StableLM reports both accuracy and normalized accuracy for some tasks, you average them—does StableLM do the same? Could you share exact prompts and evaluation harness versions for a strictly apples-to-apples comparison?

questions.title: What happens to training dynamics when many weights quantize to 0—do parameters get 'stuck' and how are they reactivated?
questions.question_body: With ternary quantization, weights near zero can flip to exactly 0. Are there mechanisms (e.g., latent FP shadow weights updated in FP, or STE ranges) that allow such weights to move away from 0 later if needed? Do you observe any dead-weight phenomena or training instabilities caused by massed zeros early in training?
